title: Harvey CEO Winston Weinberg: How to Make Mega Deals
author: Winston Weinberg

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Weinberg supports the proposition that corporate legal departments use AI for work distinct from law-firm work and may stop paying outside counsel for selected tasks, while total legal activity and fees can still grow. His claims are forecasts and anecdotal rather than evidence of universal insourcing or employment effects.
qs: interesting about our business is a lot of the work that we're doing for like a corporate is not the work that our law firm customers are doing.
But there are certain things I don't want to pay for anymore,  right?

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Weinberg’s account supports the cluster’s proposition through a narrow early demonstration: Harvey placed a legal-specific workflow on top of GPT-3 and had practising landlord–tenant attorneys review whether generated answers were usable. This aligns with lawyer–engineer product layering and human verification, but it does not establish general accuracy, durable specialist value or autonomous legal-service capability.
qs: Um, what we had basically done was we got went on r/legaladvice, which is basically like a subreddit for asking real questions, and we grabbed a bunch of those questions, ran a chain of thought product that we had basically built on top of it, and gave it to a bunch of landlord-tenant attorneys.
And then we basically said just like, "Look at these questions and tell me if they're you would send the answer." We didn't say anything about AI to the consumer who asked the question.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Weinberg supports the proposition that AI will reallocate and devalue routine legal production rather than eliminate lawyers. His private-equity anecdote describes spending shifting away from routine tasks toward new advisory needs, while his broader claim that demand will grow is explicitly a forecast rather than measured employment evidence.
qs: But there's all these new things that I'm paying law firms for.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: Weinberg directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that founder-led oversight and firefighting become constraints as a company scales. He argues for trusted leadership, a reliably operating organisation, sharper prioritisation and renewed founder focus on product. His claims are experiential rather than systematic evidence, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caveats.
qs: And like that's really what I'm trying to do this year is transition from kind of all those heroics to can you build a really well-run machine?
Like you cannot scale a really good company and get to tens of billions of revenue if you have constant trust issues and you can't trust other leadership, right?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Weinberg broadly supports selective deployment and work redesign: he stresses that fragmented enterprise systems make end-to-end agentic execution difficult, that adoption depends on integration and user capability, and that AI is more likely to shift routine work while generating new legal demand than eliminate lawyers wholesale. His account is more commercially optimistic than the synthesis and relies mainly on forecasts, customer anecdotes and reported business experience rather than independent evidence on productivity, verification or labour effects.
qs: And so, the long tail on actually getting these systems and agents to do a  task from start to finish is so difficult.

And so, I think people think about this and they're like, "Oh, wow, like AI is going to impact legal and it's going to just destroy all these jobs." The thing they aren't thinking about is all of their customers are using AI to create more products.

kp.k: Frontier models threaten insufficiently differentiated legal AI products
kp.d: Weinberg identifies product-development speed as Harvey's principal existential concern. His argument is not that model providers will immediately concentrate resources on law, but that general enterprise offerings will reduce vertical applications' value unless those applications maintain substantial differentiation and solve customers' frontier problems.
qs: the value of your product is going to go down unless there is a massive delta between what your product does and what you could get from an enterprise GPT license, right?
how do you make sure you get to like escape velocity on product, so you have enough of a product moat for them to not run you over.

kp.k: Harvey routes work across models despite OpenAI investment
kp.d: Weinberg reports routing use cases to combinations of models, with traffic to Opus 4.5 increasing significantly but not becoming a majority at the interview date. He says OpenAI's investment imposes no contractual or relational requirement to use its models, and portrays application-provider feedback about comparative performance as valuable to model developers.
qs: we route basically based off of the use case, we route to the best combination of models and definitely our traffic went up to Opus 4.5 significantly.
Well, we aren't routing the majority yet, but even if we were, there's no conflict.
there's nothing in like our agreement or our relationship or anything like that that you have to use OpenAI models.

kp.k: Enterprise productivity depends on integration, not only model improvements
kp.d: Weinberg distinguishes a perceived consumer-performance plateau from continuing enterprise and code-generation improvements. He predicts massive enterprise productivity gains in three to five years, arguing that existing capabilities already exceed adoption. His illustrative workflows span 17 or sometimes 50 systems, making end-to-end agent deployment difficult even within vertical markets.
qs: I think that we're seeing a plateau in performance for consumer use cases.
I think like three to five years um until we see like massive, massive productivity gains in enterprise.
The capabilities were there two years ago, right?
the long tail on actually getting these systems and agents to do a task from start to finish is so difficult.

kp.k: Legal workflows spread AI adoption across corporate departments
kp.d: Weinberg reports adoption by tax compliance and procurement departments despite limited features specifically built for them. He attributes this expansion to legal documents' centrality across enterprises. Shared Spaces was initially intended to connect corporate clients and law firms, but he says it also supports collaboration among internal legal, compliance, HR and other departments.
qs: Starting to happen is those departments are adopting Harvey even though we haven't built features specifically for those departments.
legal documents are such a core part of a business that they interact with all of these different parts of the business, right?
the like legal team is working with the compliance department is working with HR, is working with everything else all in Harvey at the same time.

kp.k: Cross-organisation collaboration requires extensive security and permissions
kp.d: Weinberg says serving banks and allowing either corporate legal teams or law firms to initiate collaboration demanded substantial security and permissioning work. Responding to the host's reported allegation that Shared Spaces copied Legora, he denies copying and says development took six months to almost a year, with permissions preceding the interface. This is his account of product development, not independently established evidence about the dispute.
qs: We were working on multiplayer a long time ago.
we're allowing the in-house side to kick it off or the law firm side.
We were going on for like six months to almost a year. We just did all the permissioning and all of that stuff first before you do kind of the UI and on top.

kp.k: Infrastructure shortcomings can undermine rapid legal AI growth
kp.d: Weinberg reports that adding tens of thousands of users in late 2023 exposed infrastructure limitations and slowed shipping in early 2024. He says almost 40% of Harvey's EPD organisation now comprises very senior infrastructure engineers and estimates processing almost half a billion documents in the preceding year. He presents scalable infrastructure, rather than attractive demonstrations alone, as necessary for supporting large-scale agentic workloads.
qs: something that kind of slowed down our shipping velocity is we added just tens of thousands of users in like the Q4 before that, right?
And we didn't quite have the infrastructure like to support that.
it's almost like 40% of our entire EPD org is very senior from like a Databricks or something like that infrastructure engineers.
for us I think last year we almost did like half a billion documents or something like that

kp.k: Retention and implementation matter more than acquisition alone
kp.d: Weinberg recommends prioritising gross revenue retention rather than judging AI vendors mainly by net new ARR. He predicts a reckoning beyond a hundred million ARR for companies unable to fulfil implementation and infrastructure promises. Using Microsoft and Databricks as analogies, he advocates post-sales investment because retained customers could purchase much more as AI products expand; the million-to-hundred-million customer example is a hypothetical upside, not a reported result.
qs: What I would tell them actually is your GRR matters.
if you don't have the infrastructure in place and you make a bunch of promises up front and then all of that falls down, you'll start losing company customers really really fast.

it's more important than landing new customers and getting really high ARR is can you retain those customers because that customer that pays you a million today, there's a real world in which they pay you a hundred million at some point.

kp.k: Law firms use custom AI to win business
kp.d: Weinberg rejects the assumption that hourly billing makes law firms unreceptive to efficiency software. He identifies fixed fees as one possible mechanism but does not expect rapid adoption. More immediately, he reports customers winning engagements with custom Harvey solutions, framing AI as a revenue-generation tool rather than merely a cost reducer. His million-dollar subscription and twenty-million-dollar engagement illustration is not documented as a specific measured case.
qs: One, they might switch to fixed fees. Well, now we're good to go and efficiency is really good. I don't think it's going to happen that fast.
we have so many law firm customers that have gained new business by building something custom in Harvey
this product that I'm paying maybe like a million dollars for a year just earned me a deal that's 20 million.

kp.k: Vendor pricing could align with expanding customer value
kp.d: Weinberg counters the host's customer-lock-in framing with a Palantir-style argument that vendors can earn more by creating greater customer value. He views corporate legal time savings as a clearer cost-saving proposition than law-firm efficiency and anticipates consumption-based pricing in parts of Harvey's business. He disputes the host's premise that customers necessarily insist on predictable seat pricing; no quantified willingness-to-pay evidence is supplied.
qs: the more value that you create for the customer, the higher you get paid.
And then on the in-house side it's even clearer. It's just if you time save time, you're saving tons of money.
there are a lot of areas where we are going to start moving to consumption based pricing and I think for at least for us, for our customer base, that would be completely fine with them.

kp.k: Corporate AI spending reaches professional-services budgets
kp.d: Weinberg reports that a couple of corporate customers fund Harvey from professional-services rather than technology budgets, giving access to substantially larger spending pools. He distinguishes this from spending on internal personnel and says much of the corporate work involved is lower-end work associated with alternative legal service providers, rather than the work performed by Harvey's law-firm customers. This is a vendor account of budget shifts, not a quantified displacement study.
qs: there are a couple companies that have basically said that the Harvey budget comes out of their spend on professional services, not out of their tech budget.
the budget for professional services is in the billions a year versus the tech budget for that G&A group is astronomically smaller.
a lot of the work that we're doing for like a corporate is not the work that our law firm customers are doing. It's like alternative legal service providers. It's this like lower end work.

kp.k: Harvey serves both law firms and corporate buyers
kp.d: Weinberg estimates that approximately 40% of revenue comes from in-house corporate customers and 60% from law firms. He expects a similar split in five years and relates it to his view of the distribution of lawyers between those settings. These are approximate company-reported shares and a forecast, not externally verified market measurements.
qs: I think it's around 40% of our revenue is in-house corporate and 60% is law firm, something like that.
I think it'll be similar. I think it'll be the same.

kp.k: Weinberg predicts demand growth rather than junior displacement
kp.d: Asked about cannibalisation of junior lawyers, Weinberg predicts more work rather than job destruction. He argues that AI-driven client product development and international expansion will create additional product-law and regulatory needs, with professional services continuing to grow alongside GDP. He expressly presents this as his gut view and an economy-wide forecast, not employment evidence or a detailed account of junior staffing and training.
qs: I I don't think so. I think we'll just get more work.
There's so many new pieces of work for professional services that my gut is that's not what's going to happen.
I think what's going to happen is the professional services market is going to actually keep growing at the same as GDP.
all of their customers are using AI to create more products. What happens when you create more products? You need more product legal advice.

kp.k: Clients may reject routine fees while buying new advice
kp.d: Weinberg recounts a conversation with a large private-equity firm expecting a strong M&A year and higher overall legal spending, while rejecting charges for some routine tasks such as NDA mark-ups. In that customer's reported framing, new demands include AI risk and country-specific regulatory issues. The anecdote illustrates changing composition of demand, not an established market-wide fee trend.
qs: whenever we have a big year, we pay more in legal fees.
Like there are certain parts of the deal etc. that I just marking up NDAs, whatever it is. I don't want to pay for that anymore, right?
But there's all these new things that I'm paying law firms for. Like AI risk, like should you buy this company?

kp.k: Geographic expansion requires local teams and product localisation
kp.d: Weinberg credits Legora's European execution and says Harvey should have invested more locally in 2023. He attributes the initial constraint to bandwidth and describes increased investment in 2025 and 2026, with better teams, partnerships and localisation. He recommends partnering with regions and industries rather than assuming knowledge from San Francisco, and notes that European hiring requires longer planning horizons.
qs: one of the things that I would have done differently in the beginning is just invest like more in Europe in like 2023, right?
you really need to partner with an industry or you need to partner with a geography, right?
how our product is localized for each geo is just a huge difference, but you can't do this from sitting in San Francisco
In Europe, you have to plan out more, right?

kp.k: Differentiation combines conventional software and specialised AI talent
kp.d: Weinberg predicts that application companies initially dependent on underlying models will differentiate through both ordinary software engineering and custom AI solutions using newly accessible proprietary data. He argues that AI research talent will consequently become important again as enterprise demands grow, and says Harvey has only recently reached the scale to hire people for this frontier work.
qs: a lot of just the core software that they build, it's not even going to be AI related. It's just core software building. And that's actually going to be much very differentiated.
none of these companies have access to proprietary data until very recently, right?
as these companies scale and they have to create more differentiated products, I think having AI talent is going to matter again.

kp.k: Early legal testing supported Harvey's initial investor approach
kp.d: Weinberg describes taking questions from r/legaladvice, generating answers using a GPT-3-based chain-of-thought product, and asking landlord–tenant attorneys whether they would send the answers. He mentions 86 out of 100 questions, but the transcript does not complete the outcome statement, so it does not establish a precise success metric. He says the results prompted a cold email to Sam Altman and Jason Kwon and a pitch to OpenAI leadership on July 4, 2022; this was an informal founder-reported exercise, not a specified independent benchmark.
qs: we grabbed a bunch of those questions, ran a chain of thought product that we had basically built on top of it, and gave it to a bunch of landlord-tenant attorneys.
Look at these questions and tell me if they're you would send the answer.
And of 86 out of 100 questions, And we cobbled all that together
we had a final pitch to kind of the rest of the Open AI C-suite actually the morning of July 4th, uh, 2022.

kp.k: Harvey aims to become core legal workflow infrastructure
kp.d: For the following year, Weinberg prioritises integrating separate product lines into an industry-critical platform rather than remaining optional productivity software. He reports 74% DAU/MAU among users of four-plus product lines, while qualifying that this group is very small and doubling each quarter. His ambition is approximately 75% DAU/MAU through integration; the reported subgroup engagement should not be read as platform-wide usage.
qs: what I want to switch from is a productivity software that is like a nice-to-have to to closer to like an operating system that is like pretty much crucial to the industry, right?
our DAU over MAU for people that use four plus product lines is 74%.
The percentage of people that have used four plus products is very low and it's doubling every quarter.
now I want to combine all of them together so we can get to that 75% DAU over MAU.

kp.k: Rapid AI growth still requires conventional organisational discipline
kp.d: Weinberg describes a cycle from product–market fit to company–market fit and renewed product development. Although AI businesses grow on compressed timelines and require some different structures, he says conventional scaling disciplines still apply, including executive hiring, sales capacity and ramp planning. He acknowledges that delayed senior appointments caused problems and created room for competitors, and recommends replacing founder heroics with delegation, ownership and painful prioritisation.
qs: Stage two is like company market fit.
I took too long to hire senior execs in some instances and it caused us problems. It created competitors when there shouldn't have been competitors
it's these really core like laws of physics about companies that remains the same. Like there's no different in AI.
there's has to be a couple really good ideas that you say no to.

kp.k: Capital and investor prestige do not guarantee market leadership
kp.d: Weinberg disputes venture-capital 'king making': capital cannot compensate for wrong product decisions, and most Harvey customers do not know leading Silicon Valley investor brands. He concedes some trust and recruitment benefits, suggesting that private-equity brand EQT can resonate more with lawyers. His broader recommendation is to select trusted investment partners rather than maximise valuation, and to assess talent beyond prestigious resumes.
qs: The vast majority of our customers don't know who Sequoia, A16Z, or any of these people even are, right?
More capital does not mean you run a better business.
someone like EQT actually gives you that more than Silicon Valley because they're private equity
we probably could have gotten much higher valuations than we took. And instead we chose the best investors and the ones that I trusted and personally wanted to work with.

kp.k: Strategic dealmaking prioritises value over routine negotiation
kp.d: Weinberg recommends listening to identify counterparties' objectives and declining to haggle when one strategically valuable outcome outweighs other terms. He describes accepting unattractive financial or other provisions to unlock subsequent deals and uses Microsoft's partnership ecosystem as an analogy. He extends this principle to hiring demonstrably best-in-class people, while acknowledging that accurately identifying such talent is a separate difficulty.
qs: One is listen more than you speak
there are certain deals where you want one thing from the deal and nothing else matters.
This only works when you understand the value of something more than everyone else does, right?
Microsoft has actually won in a lot of areas because they've decided to partner with kind of everyone

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Winston Weinberg predicts expanding legal demand rather than junior-lawyer displacement, and describes AI as a source of new business, changed purchasing patterns and increasingly integrated enterprise workflows.
pts.d: C1 — Employment and demand: Weinberg rejects the suggestion that AI will cannibalize junior lawyers. He expects more work and professional-services growth in line with GDP as clients use AI to create products and expand internationally, generating product, regulatory and AI-risk advice. He acknowledges that clients will no longer want to pay for certain routine tasks and that bankruptcy and some litigation are countercyclical. C2 — Law-firm economics: He says firms already win business by building custom Harvey solutions and using them in pitches, including M&A. Fixed fees could make efficiency directly valuable, but he does not expect a rapid switch away from hourly billing. C3 — In-house economics and purchasing: He says time savings reduce corporate legal costs and that some companies already fund Harvey from professional-services rather than technology budgets. He characterizes much of the corporate work involved as lower-end work otherwise performed by ALSPs, rather than work performed by Harvey's law-firm customers. C4 — Vendor pricing and value: He expects movement toward consumption-based pricing in Harvey's market and believes customers will accept it. More broadly, he predicts dramatically rising B2B software value and greater alignment between vendor compensation and customer ROI; his example of a customer eventually increasing annual spend from one million to one hundred million dollars is a possibility, not a reported outcome. C5 — Enterprise collaboration: He reports that Harvey adoption is spreading from legal departments into tax, compliance, procurement, HR and other functions even without dedicated features. Shared Spaces supports both corporate–law-firm collaboration and collaboration inside corporations. C6 — Productivity: He predicts major enterprise productivity gains as existing AI capabilities become integrated into workflows; fragmented systems and end-to-end agent implementation, rather than model capabilities alone, constrain realization. C7 — Competition and differentiation: He says improving foundation-model products threaten legal-AI application vendors unless their products offer substantially more than an enterprise GPT license. He expects differentiation increasingly to depend on core software, infrastructure and custom AI solutions using proprietary data. C8 — Scale and retention: He predicts that inadequate infrastructure and implementation will cause customer losses at fast-growing AI vendors. He presents retention and expansion of existing accounts as more consequential than new sales alone. C9 — Harvey's direction: He aims to turn Harvey from optional productivity software into an integral industry platform where lawyers conduct their daily work, by combining its existing product lines. C10 — Market composition: He reports approximately 60% law-firm and 40% corporate in-house revenue and expects a similar split in five years.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source primarily offers Weinberg's customer experience, internal company metrics and economic reasoning; it does not present independent labor-market or productivity research.
pts.d: C1 — Weinberg bases his employment and demand forecast on economic reasoning and a recent conversation with an unnamed large private-equity firm about rising aggregate legal fees alongside reduced willingness to pay for routine work. He explicitly describes his conclusion as his gut view; no employment dataset or quantified demand model is supplied. C2 — He reports multiple customers winning work with custom Harvey solutions, but supplies no named transaction or independently documented case. The one-million-dollar software purchase leading to a twenty-million-dollar deal is framed illustratively, not as a documented customer outcome. C3–C5 — Budget substitution and cross-department adoption are reported firsthand customer observations without customer-level figures or named budget examples. The claim that time savings save money is economic reasoning, not a measured cost study. C4 — Consumption-pricing acceptance is based on what he says he has seen in Harvey's vertical; future ROI and account expansion are predictions. C6 — He argues that existing capabilities are underused and describes workflows requiring data from many systems; the transcript provides no enterprise productivity experiment. C7 — His account of rising model capabilities includes Harvey routing significantly more traffic to Opus 4.5, while explicitly denying that a majority of traffic had shifted to Anthropic. No comparative model benchmark is provided. C8 — He cites Harvey's own infrastructure bottlenecks after adding tens of thousands of users in late 2023, slower shipping in early 2024, an engineering/product/design organization with almost 40% senior infrastructure engineers, and roughly half a billion documents processed in the previous year. These are self-reported operational figures. C9 — His platform ambition is supported by a reported 74% daily-active/monthly-active-user ratio among users of four or more product lines; he qualifies that this cohort is very small, though doubling quarterly. This is engagement evidence, not a measure of legal accuracy or productivity. C10 — The revenue split is an approximate internal figure, with the five-year forecast justified by his impression of the distribution of lawyers between firms and corporations. Separately, Weinberg recounts an early GPT-3 prototype exercise using 100 r/legaladvice questions reviewed by landlord–tenant attorneys for whether they would send the answers. He mentions 86 out of 100, but the supplied transcript leaves the result sentence incomplete; it therefore does not clearly establish a formal accuracy or approval rate. No sampling protocol, controls or independent validation are given.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Weinberg distinguishes changes already observed from three-to-five-year productivity expectations, a five-year revenue-mix forecast and a next-year platform ambition; many broader predictions have no firm deadline.
pts.d: The supplied document dates the interview to 2026; relative dates are interpreted on that basis. C1 — The no-cannibalization and expanding-demand forecast has no precise horizon and depends on broader AI-driven economic growth generating additional legal needs. He allows for short economic disruptions and differences between practice areas. C2 — AI-assisted business wins are described as already happening; fixed-fee adoption is possible but not expected quickly. C3 — Professional-services budget substitution is already occurring at a couple of companies. C4 — Consumption-based pricing and rising software ROI are future developments without specific deadlines; aligning the product with customer value is an explicit condition. C5 — Cross-functional adoption and Shared Spaces collaboration are current observations. Corporate and law-firm initiation of shared work required extensive security and permissioning development, which he says took roughly six months to almost a year. C6 — He places massive enterprise productivity gains three to five years ahead, approximately 2029–2031. He says capabilities are already available and were available two years earlier, but connecting fragmented systems and enabling agents to finish tasks remains difficult. His adjacent code-generation forecast is for faster improvement over the next 12 months. C7 — Model-provider pressure is continuous; he expects winners and losers in many AI markets to be decided within the next couple of years, without identifying guaranteed legal-market winners. Differentiation through proprietary-data solutions and AI talent is an evolving requirement as application vendors scale. C8 — His predicted infrastructure reckoning is associated with vendors passing approximately $100 million ARR, not a calendar deadline. C9 — The move to an integral platform is his ambition for the following year, approximately 2027, rather than a demonstrated present condition. The targeted approximately 75% DAU/MAU should not be confused with the existing 74% figure for a small multi-product cohort. C10 — He expects the current approximate 60/40 law-firm/in-house revenue split to remain similar five years later, approximately 2031. The prototype exercise is retrospective and precedes the July 4, 2022 OpenAI pitch.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims principally concern commercial law firms, corporate legal buyers, ALSP work and legal-AI vendors, rather than public access to legal assistance.
pts.d: C1–C2 — Junior lawyers are explicitly included in Weinberg's prediction against displacement. Commercial law firms and professional-services providers face less demand for paid routine tasks but, in his account, greater demand for AI-risk, product and regulatory advice as clients grow. Firms using custom AI solutions may win mandates from competing firms. No staffing ratios, associate promotion changes or practice-specific employment estimates are offered. C3 — Corporate in-house legal departments are the buyers gaining time and cost savings and potentially reallocating external professional-services expenditure to software. ALSPs are identified as providers of the lower-end work involved, suggesting potential substitution for their services, but Weinberg does not quantify ALSP revenue or employment losses. Harvey is the software vendor in this account, not itself identified as an ALSP. C4 — Vendors could capture more revenue as customer value and usage expand; corporate and law-firm customers may encounter consumption-based purchasing rather than exclusively seat-based pricing. C5 — Legal teams, outside counsel and adjacent enterprise functions can collaborate in the same environment. Large corporations, including Global 2000 and Fortune 500 businesses, are especially prominent; banks exemplify demanding security and permissioning requirements. C6 — Enterprise workers and businesses more broadly are the intended beneficiaries of integrated agents and productivity gains. C7–C8 — Legal-AI application vendors face competition from foundation-model providers, operational scaling requirements and retention risks. Their engineering and AI-research teams must build infrastructure and differentiated products, while customers depend on successful implementation and reliability. C9–C10 — Lawyers using Harvey are the intended users of an everyday work platform, with both law firms and in-house departments expected to remain substantial customer groups. The landlord–tenant prototype concerns individual legal questions, but the interview does not make a concrete access-to-justice forecast or claim that the prototype establishes safe unsupervised legal advice.
